A species of tiny human has been discovered, which lived on the remote Indonesian island of Flores just 18,000 years ago. . . . Researchers have so far unearthed remains from eight individuals who were just one metre tall, with grapefruit-sized skulls. These astonishing little people . . . made tools, hunted tiny elephants and lived at the same time as modern humans who were colonizing the area. —Nature, October 2004 Light: lifted, I stretch my brief body. Color: blaze of day behind blank eyes. Sound: birds stab greedy beaks Into trunk and seed, spill husk Onto the heap where my dreaming And my loving live. Every day I wake to this. Tracks follow the heavy beasts Back to where they huddle, herd. Hunt: a dance against hunger. Music: feast and fear. This island becomes us. Trees cap our sky. It rustles with delight In a voice green as lust. Reptiles Drag night from their tails, Live by the dark. A rage of waves Protects the horizon, which we would devour. One day I want to dive in and drift, Legs and arms wracked with danger. Like a dark star. I want to last.

outputs.L1:
A tiny human species has been discovered that lived on the remote Indonesian island of Flores as recently as 18,000 years ago. Researchers have so far unearthed the remains of eight individuals, each only one metre tall and possessing a grapefruit-sized skull. These astonishing little people made tools, hunted tiny elephants, and lived alongside modern humans who were colonizing the area.  
—*Nature*, October 2004

Light: lifted, I stretch  
my brief body.

Color: the blaze of day  
behind blank eyes.

Sound: birds stab greedy beaks  
into trunk and seed, spilling husks  
onto the heap where my dreaming  
and my loving live.

Every day, I wake to this.

Tracks follow the heavy beasts  
back to where they huddle—the herd.

Hunt: a dance against hunger.  
Music: feast and fear.

This island becomes us.  
Trees cap our sky. It rustles with delight  
in a voice as green as lust.

Reptiles drag night from their tails,  
living by the dark.

A rage of waves protects the horizon,  
which we would devour.

One day, I want to dive in and drift,  
legs and arms wracked with danger.

Like a dark star,  
I want to last.
outputs.L2:
On the isolated Indonesian island of Flores, scientists discovered a diminutive human species that survived until only 18,000 years ago. Thus far, they have recovered the remains of eight individuals, each approximately one metre tall and possessing a skull no larger than a grapefruit. Remarkably, these small humans fashioned tools, hunted miniature elephants, and shared the region with modern humans then settling there. —*Nature*, October 2004

Morning raises me,  
and my small frame unfolds.  
Day burns in colors  
my unseeing eyes cannot hold.  

Birds drive hungry bills  
through bark and fruit, scattering shells  
across the mound that shelters  
my sleep and desire.  
This is how each day begins.  

Footprints lead us after  
the ponderous animals  
to the place where they gather close.  
The chase is hunger given movement;  
our songs carry terror and plenty.  

We belong to this island,  
and it belongs within us.  
Branches seal the heavens overhead,  
whispering their vivid pleasure  
in a language lush with longing.  

Lizards trail darkness behind them  
and thrive beneath its cover.  
Furious water guards the farthest edge—  
a boundary we ache to consume.  

Someday I will plunge into that sea  
and let it bear me outward,  
my limbs strained by peril,  
drifting like a shadowed sun.  

I wish to remain.
outputs.L3:
Researchers discovered the remains of eight unusually small humans who lived on the Indonesian island of Flores about 18,000 years ago. Standing roughly one metre tall and possessing skulls about the size of a grapefruit, these Flores humans nevertheless demonstrated considerable skill and adaptability. They made tools, hunted small elephants, and survived alongside modern humans who were colonizing the region.

The poem inspired by their lives presents island existence as a continuous cycle of awakening, hunting, hunger, celebration, fear, and close contact with the natural world. Nature is both sustaining and threatening, shaping every aspect of the community’s daily experience. Against this backdrop, the speaker expresses a desire to cross the ocean horizon that protects and confines the island. Although such a journey would involve great danger, it represents the hope of escaping isolation and achieving a more permanent, enduring existence.
outputs.L4:
Researchers excavating a cave on the Indonesian island of Flores uncovered the remains of eight unusually small humans, each only about one metre tall. These ancient people, now known as *Homo floresiensis*, had small brains but were capable toolmakers and skilled hunters. Evidence suggests that they pursued animals, prepared food, gathered around fires, and adapted successfully to the island’s distinctive and sometimes dangerous environment.

The poem imaginatively brings their lost world to life through vivid sensory details: the sounds of the hunt, the smell of cooking meat, the excitement of feasting, and the constant threat posed by predators and the landscape. Rather than presenting the Flores people merely as scientific specimens, it portrays them as a community with fear, courage, appetite, memory, and a powerful instinct to survive.

The discovery was especially significant because these people appear to have lived as recently as 18,000 years ago, meaning that they may have shared the world—and perhaps Flores itself—with modern humans. Their existence challenges the assumption that *Homo sapiens* was the only surviving human species in the recent past and reveals that human evolution was more varied and complex than previously believed. By giving an imaginative voice to the island’s vanished inhabitants, the poem also expresses a poignant desire not to disappear completely: although the people themselves are gone, their bones, tools, and reconstructed experiences allow them to be remembered.
outputs.L5:
### Researchers Explore Indonesia’s Remarkable Island of Flores

Flores, an Indonesian island in the eastern part of the archipelago, continues to attract researchers from around the world. Its volcanic landscapes, diverse ecosystems, and rich cultural traditions make it an important location for scientific study.

Archaeologists have gained valuable insights into human history through discoveries on Flores, including evidence of *Homo floresiensis*, an ancient human relative known for its small stature. Researchers also study the island’s unique wildlife, geology, languages, and traditional communities.

Indonesian researchers play a central role in these projects, often collaborating with international universities and scientific institutions. Their work not only expands our understanding of Flores but also supports conservation efforts and helps preserve the island’s archaeological and cultural heritage for future generations.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem inspired by the 2004 discovery of Homo floresiensis, beginning with a brief epigraph from Nature and imagining life from the perspective of one of these ancient island inhabitants.
counterfactuals.output:
> “A new small-bodied hominin from the Late Pleistocene of Flores, Indonesia.”  
> —*Nature*, 2004

**Liang Bua, Before the Name**

I wake where the cave keeps  
a little of yesterday’s fire  
under its black tongue.

Outside, Flores steams—  
leaf, vine, volcanic stone,  
the morning opening  
one wet green hand.

I am not small to myself.

The grass rises to my waist,  
the sky is as far  
as any sky must be,  
and my shadow, walking before me,  
knows no measure.

We follow the river’s rumor  
toward the place where stegodons  
press their round feet into mud.  
Their calves are mountains  
we can imagine carrying.

I hold a sharpened stone.  
It fits my palm  
as if the earth had broken  
to give me an answer.

There are dragons here.

They wait like fallen branches,  
then breathe.  
Their mouths make sudden weather.  
We know the trees that save us,  
the paths too narrow for hunger,  
the hour when scales grow slow  
beneath the cooling sun.

At dusk we bring meat home,  
tubers, red fruit,  
stories without names.

A child taps bone on stone.  
Someone laughs.  
Someone tends the flame  
until the cave walls tremble  
with our enormous shapes.

We do not know  
an island can be called an island.

We do not know  
the sea is keeping us,  
or keeping others away.

We do not know extinction,  
species, specimen,  
the careful brush  
lifting darkness from a brow.

I know only this:

my sister sleeping near the ashes,  
rain stitching the forest shut,  
the warm tool beside my hand,  
and beyond the cave  
the long, low cry of something  
alive enough to fear.

Many ages from now  
you will enter softly.

You will find one skull,  
some bones,  
stones touched into purpose.

You will call us lost.

But tonight  
the fire knows our faces.

Tonight  
we are the ones  
who remain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lyrical first-person poem about the “hobbit” people of Flores: their small bodies, hunting of tiny elephants, tropical surroundings, isolation, and desire to endure. Include the scientific discovery announcement as an opening quotation.
counterfactuals.output:
> “A new small-bodied hominin from the Late Pleistocene of Flores, Indonesia.”

We were the little people of the green fire,  
knee-high to shadow, quick beneath the leaves,  
our island cupped in the ocean’s enormous hand,  
its volcano breathing through woven clouds.

We walked where orchids drank the rain,  
where dragons furrowed the riverbanks,  
and palms beat softly in the monsoon wind.  
Stone by stone, we sharpened hunger  
into an edge bright enough to live.

We followed the tiny elephants—  
young stegodons moving like gray hills  
through fern and bamboo—  
and carried their thunder home in pieces,  
meat for the dark, bone for remembrance,  
smoke lifting our names toward the canopy.

The sea kept other worlds away.  
Around us, blue distance without a bridge;  
within us, the old flame refusing silence.  
Small were our bodies, not our wanting.  
We knew the lean season, ashfall, storm,  
the long teeth waiting beyond the firelight.

Still, I say we sang.  
Still, I say our children woke  
to fruit-sweet mornings and cicada choirs.  
We pressed our footprints into Flores  
as if the earth might learn us by heart.

Call me hobbit, relic, mystery—  
a skull lifted gently from the cave’s cool sleep.  
I was more than what endured in stone.  
I was a hand around another hand,  
an ember guarded through tropical rain,  
a small voice telling the immense night:

**We are here.  
We have been here.  
We mean to remain.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Using the Nature report about eight one-metre-tall humans found on Flores as an epigraph, compose an evocative poem that contrasts sensory island imagery with hunger, danger, love, and mortality.
counterfactuals.output:
### **Flores, After the Small People**

*“The remains of eight humans, about one metre tall, were found on Flores.”*  
—paraphrased from a report in *Nature*

Morning opens a green mouth:  
fern, pandanus, the wet metallic cry  
of birds stitching sunlight  
through the canopy.

The sea breathes salt into the caves.  
Orchids cup last night’s rain.  
Under the fig trees, fruit hangs  
purple as bruises—

but hunger is a patient animal.  
It follows the small ones over stone,  
counts the ribs beneath their skin,  
licks the marrow of every shadow.

Beyond the reeds, the giant stork  
lifts its spear of a beak.  
Komodo dragons drag their bellies  
through the leaf-rot, slow as fire.

Still, a hand finds another hand.

In the cave’s cool throat  
someone tends a flame;  
someone divides the bitter root,  
gives the sweeter half away.

Perhaps love was no larger than this:  
a shoulder pressed close in rain,  
a name breathed against darkness,  
a child carried when the path grew sharp.

Outside, Flores blazed—  
turquoise water, red hibiscus,  
volcanoes shouldering clouds  
like gods who would not look down.

And death came without wonder,  
through fever, tooth, or falling ash,  
closing each bright, hungering body  
at the measure of one metre.

Yet the limestone kept them:  
eight silences beneath the earth,  
eight small doors through which we see  
how little flesh a life requires,

how vast the fear,  
how fierce the tenderness,  
how the island, fragrant and dangerous,  
goes on flowering over every grave.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine you are a member of Homo floresiensis living 18,000 years ago. Write a compact free-verse dramatic monologue describing waking, tracking prey, hunting, feasting, observing birds and reptiles, and dreaming of crossing the sea.
counterfactuals.output:
I wake beneath the limestone roof,  
ash cold between my fingers,  
dawn spilling green through the vines.

In wet earth I find the marks—  
deer, small and quick—  
and follow with stone in hand,  
my hunger walking before me.

We drive it toward the narrow ground.  
A spear leaps.  
The forest shudders, then is still.

Tonight fat hisses in the fire.  
We crack bone, share marrow,  
paint our mouths with smoke and blood.

Above us, giant storks fold their wings.  
A lizard, long as a fallen tree,  
tastes the dark with its tongue.

Beyond the beach  
the sea keeps shining—  
a blue animal no spear can hold.

I sleep and dream  
we lash wood to wood,  
push past the last black reef,  
and follow the birds  
to another fire  
burning under another sky.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Turn the discovery of the Flores “tiny humans” into a literary poem. Preserve a journalistic excerpt at the start, then shift into fragmented, image-rich verse with motifs of light, color, sound, music, waves, and the longing to survive.
counterfactuals.output:
**FLORES, INDONESIA — NEWS BRIEF**

*Archaeologists excavating Liang Bua cave on the island of Flores have uncovered the remains of a previously unknown human species. Standing roughly one metre tall, the small-bodied hominins lived as recently as 50,000 years ago. Stone tools and animal bones found nearby suggest they hunted, made fire, and survived for generations in isolation. Researchers have named the species* Homo floresiensis. *The discovery challenges long-held assumptions about human evolution.*

---

They entered the earth  
with brushes,  
with lamps trembling in their hands—

and the earth answered  
in ochre.

A forehead.  
A wrist.  
The pale parenthesis of a rib.

Small one,  
island one,  
your skull held darkness  
the way a shell holds the sea:

not silence, exactly,

but the blue-green pulse  
of something listening.

*

Outside the cave, Flores burned—  
hibiscus, volcanic glass,  
the red throat of evening.

Dwarf elephants moved  
through spear-grass.

Komodo dragons dragged  
their ancient shadows  
over the stones.

And you—

ankle-deep in fernlight,  
a blade of flint singing  
against another blade—

made sparks.

Brief stars.  
A little weather of gold.

Perhaps that was music:

stone striking stone,  
bone tapping hollow wood,  
rain loosening itself  
from the black leaves.

Perhaps you sang.

Not words we could gather,  
not names that survived  
the long salt of years,

but a sound like waves  
entering a cavern—

returning,  
returning—

each echo smaller  
and still alive.

*

Who did you call for  
when the mountain reddened?

Who carried the child  
through ash?

Whose hand pressed soot  
into whose wound?

The sea rose around the island,  
a bright blade.

The sea fell.

The moon polished  
the same path over water  
until even the path was gone.

Yet in the chamber  
your bones kept their ember—

fifty thousand seasons  
under limestone,

while roots drank darkness  
and beetles tuned  
their minute instruments.

*

Now floodlights bloom  
where fire once breathed.

Cameras click:  
a hard rain.

Measurements, labels,  
the clean white music  
of numbers.

One metre tall.  
Small brain.  
Extinct.

But no number records  
the green astonishment  
of morning,

or how you leaned toward warmth  
when night came down  
violet and immense.

No graph contains  
the hunger in the hand,

that oldest rhythm:

reach,  
grasp,  
break,  
share.

No glass case can hold  
the fierce red thread—

I am here.  
I am here.  
Let me remain.

*

Little human,  
they call you hobbit,  
as if wonder must be softened  
into story.

But you were not a fable.

You were weather and blood,  
salt-footed, smoke-eyed,

a note struck once  
in evolution’s dark music—

low, bright,  
unresolved.

Across the ages  
the cave gives you back  
piece by piece:

jaw, femur,  
the cup of the skull—

and from that cup  
light spills,

thin as dawn  
on the Flores Strait.

Listen:

beneath the engines,  
beneath the voices  
naming and renaming you,

the waves keep time.

They say  
vanished.

The waves say  
otherwise.

They say  
small.

The stars lean closer.

And somewhere under every name  
the old song gathers—

broken, radiant—

survive,  
survive,  
survive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
